intro.text: A modern classical game in the Anti-Berlin: White plays the same calm protection of the centre pawn that this course teaches, and Black chooses a solid closed setup.
Study it from both sides. The original moves are the main line; at four critical moments engine branches show what was better, played until the engine's verdict.

claims.text: Black's view: develop and counterattack White's centre pawn at once. White's view: decide how to protect it.
White's view: protect the centre pawn with a pawn and keep a slow manoeuvring game. Black's view: there is no immediate target, so develop calmly.
Black's view: support the centre pawn with a pawn as well. The game becomes a closed Spanish where both sides improve their pieces first.
White's view: the c-pawn gives the bishop a retreat square and prepares a central advance with the d-pawn.
Later White retreats the bishop with Ba4 and finally strikes with d4.
White's view: keeping the light-squared bishop matters more than doubling Black's pawns here; it will later aim at Black's king from the other diagonal.
White's queen's knight will travel Nf1 and Ne3, the classic Spanish route.
Black's view: with White developing slowly, Black regroups too and keeps the centre closed.
White's view: a small but useful move that keeps Black's pieces away from a kingside square before the centre opens.
White's view: after full preparation White finally occupies the centre with two pawns. Black's view: keep the tension and wait for White to commit.
Black's knight goes back only to come to Nbd7, where it supports the centre and frees the bishop's path.
White's view: such a quiet retreat means White can choose the moment to change the centre.
White's pawns on d5 and e4 now lock the centre.
Both sides' view: with the centre closed, the play moves to the wings. White gains queenside space; Black looks for counterplay and a better post for the bishops.

principle.text: When the centre is locked, attack where your pawns point and where you have more space.

claims.text: White's view: more queenside space and support for the advanced pawn. Black's view: these pawns can also become targets once lines open.
The exchange has opened the b-file for the rooks.
Both sides' view: whoever controls the open file first gets the more active rooks.
Black's view: fixing White's queenside pawns gives Black's knight and bishop secure squares in front of them.
The knight continues to Ne3, eyeing the outposts on the kingside and in the centre.
Now the c-file is open as well.
White's view: the pawn on d5 is protected and cramps Black. Black's view: the squares around it are excellent posts for Black's pieces.
Black's view: the dark-squared bishop had no scope behind its own pawns, so it moves outside the pawn chain to pressure White's pieces.
Engine check: the engine prefers a different move here (see the Better was branch), though the difference is smaller than a clear mistake.
White's view: the knight wanted to regroup, but it gave Black time to advance on the kingside.
Engine check: 32.g3 weakens White's king position badly; 32.Ne3 was much better.
Black's view: once pawns are exchanged in front of White's king, Black's pieces can use the new open lines.
Engine check: keeping the queens was a little stronger (see the Better was branch); Black stays clearly better either way.
Practical view: trading queens when ahead reduces risk, even if the engine finds a stronger continuation.
Engine check: the engine finds an even stronger continuation (see the Better was branch), but Black is winning either way.
The broadcast score ends here and records a win for Black. The source does not say why White stopped, so the course does not guess.
